newsitem.title: USA: Key U.S. Democrat may vote against China MFN.
newsitem.headline: Key U.S. Democrat may vote against China MFN.

text.p: House of Representatives Minority Leader Richard Gephardt on Saturday said he might vote against renewing China's Most Favored Nation trade status this year to keep pressure on Beijing to improve human rights.
The Missouri Democrat said he opposed efforts to make China's MFN status permanent, saying annual debate on trade allowed Washington to continue raising the issue of human rights with China.

"If we don't bring up human rights in China, I don't know who will," Gephardt told CNN's "Inside Politics" program, adding, "And the truth is they've been going backwards on human rights -- not in the right direction."
Gephardt's remarks came on the day Vice President Al Gore departed for an eight-day trip to Asia aimed at easing strains in U.S.-Sino relations.

The United States should apply "constant and consistent pressure on the Chinese government to give their people human rights, to open up their political system, and to have a more democratic form of government," Gephardt said.
"I probably will vote against it because I think, again, we need to keep the pressure on the Chinese government to do the right thing," he said.
Gephardt said Congress should also be permitted to review China's accession to the World Trade Organization and said he opposed a 15-year transition to get to global tariff levels.

Gephardt said he supported Gore's trip to China, noting that while the Clinton administration's policy of constructive engagegment had not "shown great results yet," it also had not yet been in place that long. "We need to be working with the Chinese actively and constructively to try to solve these problems between us," he said.

Gephardt has been at odds with the Clinton administration on various economic issues, including renewing the North American Free Trade Agreement and revising the way the Consumer Price Index is calculated.
But he denied his positions were laying the groundwork to challenge Gore for the presidency in 2000.

"The last thing we need to be doing is starting a race that's going to happen in the year 2000 and way off in the future before we even know who's going to be involved in that race. It just isn't helpful," he said.
